items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] We know that King Oliver came up on the boat. Louis Armstrong came up. Were their names and their images a part of what you were aware of as a young man? [INTERVIEWEE] No, because we had our own group.

ctx.x: I’d be happy to. The first one, which might seem to just coincidental, being on the water – I think that because St. Louis was on the Mississippi River – I don’t – I’m not so sure. I don’t think so, that the water itself had anything to do with making it more conducive to horns playing – articulation. I don’t think that [?] to it. But the mere fact that St. Louis is on the Mississippi River, and these boats came up from New Orleans, the Streckfus steamers – St. Louis became a very, very integral part of jazz,…
Let me just ask you that. We know that King Oliver came up on the boat. Louis Armstrong came up. Were their names and their images a part of what you were aware of as a young man?

No, because we had our own group. There’s a cat who – the Lord Mayor of the whole situation was a cat named Charlie Creath, spelled c-r-e-a-t-h, but he pronounced it Charlie Creth. He called himself the King of Cornet. Charlie Creath, King of Cornet. Now he could play, man. He could swing. He could swing you into bad health, and all
